---
title: "DFS as a Mathematical State Transition"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning for algorithm interviews, with a worked example and proof."
---

## When to recognise this technique

When a problem says explore every reachable configuration, connected region or path.

## Start with the question

**What is a state, which moves are legal, and how do I avoid visiting the same state forever?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
s_{t+1}\in N(s_t),\qquad s_t\in V
$$

**Every symbol explained:** s_t is the current state at step t, V the set of all possible states, and N(s_t) the legal next states reachable in one move. The membership sign means 'belongs to'.

**Substitute actual values:** For graph A→B and A→C, DFS starting at A can visit A, then B, return to A, and then C. The new state must be a neighbour of the current state. The visited set prevents returning indefinitely.

## Why the mathematics works

DFS follows one branch until it cannot proceed, then returns. In a finite graph, marking a vertex when discovered means each vertex is expanded at most once; traversing adjacency lists costs O(V+E).

## Limits and counterexamples

Do not confuse 'find any path' (DFS works) with 'find the fewest edges' (ordinary DFS is not guaranteed optimal). Mark visited globally for reachability; for enumerating simple paths, you may instead need path-local membership and undo.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Define states, define legal transitions, define a visited invariant, then recurse. To prove completeness, argue every reachable unvisited neighbour will be explored.**

Try explaining the formula aloud using the numerical example, then reproduce the proof from memory. An interview answer must justify the relationship, not just quote it.

**Practice problems:** Number of Islands; Flood Fill.
